title: How Data Centers Broke American Politics
gist: Data center opposition has become a cross-ideological American mass movement: 70 percent of Americans oppose local construction per Gallup, Facebook opposition group membership went from under 100,000 in December to over 500,000 by July, and moratoriums have been introduced in at least a dozen states and passed in New York. The reporting's central finding is that anti-data-center sentiment and AI skepticism are the same phenomenon rather than separate ones — research shows most opponents do not live near data centers — and that the populist right, led by Steve Bannon and Joe Allen, read this convergence earlier than either Washington or the AI industry.

themes.theme: Scale and velocity of the backlash

insights.claim: A recent Gallup poll found 70 percent of Americans would somewhat or strongly oppose data center construction in their area, a level of opposition that makes local siting a default-hostile process nationwide.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Siting risk should now be priced as a base case, not a tail risk, in any hyperscaler capex or REIT development model.
insights.quote: A recent Gallup poll showed that 70 percent of Americans would somewhat oppose or strongly oppose data center construction in their area.
insights.locator: Data center resistance certainly has some of its roots

insights.claim: National membership in data center opposition groups on Facebook exploded from under 100,000 in December to more than 500,000 by July, a fivefold increase in roughly seven months.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A 5x organizing base in under a year is the leading indicator that local permitting friction converts into state legislation within one or two sessions.
insights.quote: National membership in data center opposition groups on Facebook has exploded in recent months, from under 100,000 in December to more than 500,000 by July.
insights.locator: There are a surprising number of Gage Baileys

insights.claim: Data center moratoriums have been introduced in at least a dozen states including Georgia and passed in one, New York, with additional bans or moratoriums adopted by cities and counties including deep-red Hill County, Texas.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Moratoriums spreading to red jurisdictions removes the usual partisan escape valve of relocating projects to friendlier states.
insights.locator: In the past few months, we’ve seen an attack

insights.claim: The backlash has escalated to physical violence, including an attack on pro-data-center Indianapolis council member Ron Gibson and an attack on OpenAI's Sam Altman, alongside protester arrests or removals at public meetings in New Jersey, California, Wisconsin, and Indiana.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Violence against named individuals shifts this from a permitting story to a security and personnel-risk story for operators and their political allies.
insights.locator: In the past few months, we’ve seen an attack

insights.claim: A veteran energy and environment reporter states she has never seen vitriol comparable to that directed at data centers in all her years covering the beat.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: An experienced beat reporter calling this unprecedented is a qualitative signal that standard community-relations playbooks are miscalibrated for this fight.
insights.quote: In all my years of reporting on energy and the environment, I have never seen anything like the type of vitriol leveled at data centers
insights.locator: When people ask what I’m doing in Georgia

themes.theme: Data centers and AI as one grievance

insights.claim: Research published in June found that very few people opposed to data centers actually live near one, and that most data center opponents are also skeptical of AI — collapsing the assumed distinction between NIMBY siting complaints and AI anxiety.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: If opposition is ideological rather than proximity-driven, then community benefit packages and siting concessions cannot buy it off — the standard mitigation strategy fails.
insights.quote: Research published in June of a small sample size of voters, for example, shows that very few people opposed to data centers actually live near them, and most of those who are against data centers are also skeptical of AI.
insights.locator: Anger against data centers and public anxieties about AI

insights.claim: Polling and policy conventionally treat data center anger and AI anxiety as separate topics — one environmental and civic, the other about job loss and chatbots — a framing the reporting argues is wrong.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Anyone forecasting policy risk from separate AI-sentiment and infrastructure-sentiment surveys is understating the correlated exposure.
insights.quote: Anger against data centers and public anxieties about AI are usually treated in polling and policy as separate topics
insights.locator: Anger against data centers and public anxieties

insights.claim: Data centers have become the physical, sitable, locally-contestable proxy for a diffuse fight against tech oligarchs — the movement's opportunity is precisely that a data center is a building you can zone against, unlike a model.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: AI regulation may arrive through land use and utility law rather than through AI-specific statute — watch county commissions and PUCs, not just Congress.
insights.quote: Data centers, which are bringing together the most disparate neighbors in all regions of the country, may represent an opportunity to wage a real, unified fight against tech oligarchs.
insights.locator: Data centers, which are bringing together

insights.claim: The triggering conditions were a stack of concrete grievances: Musk reportedly trucking unpermitted gas turbines into a majority-Black, already-polluted Memphis neighborhood for xAI, a widely-shared (later disputed) Washington Post estimate that one ChatGPT search consumed a bottle of water, and consumer electric bills rising as utilities forecast data center demand.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Retail electricity bills are the transmission mechanism turning abstract AI concern into voter action; utility rate cases are the venue where this shows up first.
insights.locator: Data centers began cropping up everywhere

insights.claim: The backlash was amplified by AI executives publicly stating their technology would take jobs and replace human creativity while simultaneously demanding local communities absorb the infrastructure — a self-inflicted messaging problem.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Industry rhetoric about labor displacement directly undermines the local economic-benefit case for siting, a contradiction operators have not resolved.
insights.quote: All of this as tech CEOs publicly mused about how AI would take everyone’s jobs and replace human creativity itself.
insights.locator: If you trusted various economic outlets

insights.claim: Surveillance is now a near-consensus belief in right-leaning online circles, with political influencer Hannah Cox reporting that her timeline treats data centers being built to surveil the population as an almost foregone conclusion.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Once a conspiracy framing becomes ambient rather than fringe, factual rebuttal stops working and opposition becomes structurally durable.
insights.quote: It’s, I feel like, a ubiquitous fear,
insights.locator: Cox and I have very different social media feeds

insights.claim: Two of the first national politicians to publicly attack data center development were right-wing populists Marjorie Taylor Greene and Thomas Massie, objecting to how a proposed 10-year ban on state AI regulation could be used to build data centers on private property.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Property rights, not environmentalism, was the entry point on the right — which is why preemption of state AI rules became politically radioactive.
insights.quote: Forcing eminent domain on people’s private properties to link the future Skynet is not very Republican
insights.locator: When I started reporting on data centers last year

insights.claim: At the end of 2025 a MAGA coalition led by Steve Bannon blocked the Trump administration's attempt to re-up a ban on state-level AI regulation, meaning the decisive veto on federal AI preemption came from the right, not the left.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Federal preemption of state AI law is unlikely while the populist right holds this position — the base case is fifty regulatory regimes, not one.
insights.locator: At the end of 2025, when the Trump administration

insights.claim: Bannon ran a deliberate ground-game strategy, instructing Joe Allen to speak at every church, MAGA, and Tea Party meeting that would have him to get the base engaged early.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Church and local-chapter organizing is a distribution channel neither the AI industry nor mainstream media monitors, which is why the movement's scale surprised Washington.
insights.quote: He’s going to every conference possible, meeting people ... and I told him, I want you to go to every church that asks you. I want you to go to MAGA, Tea Party meetings.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, Steve Bannon, Trump’s erstwhile former adviser

insights.claim: Bannon's War Room framed data centers as 'weapons labs' being 'turned onto the population,' language the reporter concedes read the public mood more accurately than mainstream analysis did.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: The populist right had better sentiment intelligence than institutional forecasters; their programming is a usable leading indicator for AI policy risk.
insights.quote: airing one segment last year that described data centers as “weapons labs” that are “being turned onto the population.”
insights.locator: Bannon, it seems, did a better job reading the room

insights.claim: Washington was completely unprepared for the data center backlash and for AI issues generally, per the reporting, leaving a policy vacuum that outside movements filled.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Policy vacuums get filled by whoever organizes first; the resulting rules are likely to be shaped by movement demands rather than industry negotiation.
insights.locator: When I started reporting on data centers last year

insights.claim: Mainstream conservative media has since taken over the conversation, with Tucker Carlson and Matt Walsh producing viral videos against specific projects and Nancy Mace campaigning for South Carolina governor on a yearlong moratorium.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Anti-data-center positioning is now a viable Republican primary platform, which means the policy risk compounds through the next election cycle.
insights.locator: In the weeks after I return from Georgia

insights.claim: Florida governor Ron DeSantis, an outspoken AI and data center critic, signed first-of-its-kind legislation ensuring local governments retain authority to reject data center development in their communities.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: State law affirmatively protecting local veto power is the most consequential regulatory development in the piece — it hardwires siting risk into a major growth state.
insights.locator: Nancy Mace, running for governor in South Carolina

themes.theme: Cross-ideological coalition and its fault lines

insights.claim: The resistance is uniting people from opposite ends of the political spectrum in a way the reporter has not previously observed, with a New York Times headline in early May calling data centers 'the most bipartisan issue since beer.'
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Genuinely bipartisan issues clear legislatures fast and are the hardest for corporate lobbying to split — the worst possible configuration for the industry.
insights.quote: the most bipartisan issue since beer
insights.locator: Data centers, which are bringing together

insights.claim: Coalition members are explicit that the alliance is tactical rather than ideological, with one New Jersey protester summarizing it as 'Any enemy of my enemy is, at least, my temporary ally.'
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Tactical coalitions hold only while a shared target exists; the fracture risk is real but so is the near-term legislative force.
insights.quote: Any enemy of my enemy is, at least, my temporary ally
insights.locator: At a recent anti-data-center demonstration in New Jersey

insights.claim: The coalition already fractured once at the organizational level: after pro-AI White House allies Marc Andreessen and David Sacks amplified criticism of Humans First in late March, the group split along partisan lines, with the conservative wing keeping the name and installing January 6 'Save America' rally organizer Amy Kremer as chair while Joe Allen departed.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Targeted pressure from AI-aligned political operators successfully split a bipartisan opposition group — a repeatable countermeasure worth watching for.
insights.locator: Politics comes for Humans First too

insights.claim: Despite the national split, local coalitions are holding: in Troup County, Georgia, activist Gage Bailey reports minimal partisan unrest in his 4,000-person Facebook group where right and left members are uniformly opposed to data centers and skeptical of AI.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: The movement's resilience lives at the county level where the fight is concrete, so national-level fragmentation does not reduce project-level risk.
insights.locator: Bailey’s Facebook group is still growing

insights.claim: Humans First went on to organize a national day of protest against data centers with events in nearly 150 counties across 42 states, demonstrating the movement's geographic reach after the split.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Coverage in 42 states means no significant siting market is insulated; this is national infrastructure opposition, not a regional phenomenon.
insights.quote: months from now, Humans First will organize a national day of protest against data centers, with events in nearly 150 counties across 42 states
insights.locator: I park my car in the cul-de-sac

insights.claim: The anti-data-center movement has an organizing infrastructure inherited from climate activism, with many Humans First staffers coming from climate organizing backgrounds and much of the local movement originating in Sierra Club chapters.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Experienced climate organizers bring proven tactics — records requests, ordinance campaigns, coalition-building — meaning the learning curve for opponents is already climbed.
insights.locator: Like many of the earliest folks involved

themes.theme: Company conduct is generating the opposition

insights.claim: Google was revealed as the eventual tenant of a Troup County, Georgia project, held one meeting with local environmental advocates in November, then stopped responding — while publicly citing a $1 million energy-bill partnership as community engagement.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A $1 million goodwill payment against a multibillion-dollar facility, paired with non-responsiveness, is the pattern converting neutral locals into permanent opponents.
insights.quote: I don’t see a scenario, at least in the immediate future, in which we’re going to be able to trust these tech companies
insights.locator: Bailey learned last year that Google

insights.claim: Projects are routinely announced without disclosing power consumption, water draw from local aquifers, or the eventual corporate tenant, forcing residents to reconstruct basic facts through public records requests.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Information opacity is the single most reliable generator of local opposition; mandatory disclosure is the most likely first regulatory concession.
insights.quote: There were, he says, next to no public details about the project—how much power it was going to use, how much water it might draw from the local aquifer.
insights.locator: Bailey, a Democrat with a degree in environmental science

insights.claim: Data center operators in northern Virginia's Data Center Alley declined WIRED's requests for facility access, citing security reasons, reinforcing the secrecy that fuels the surveillance narrative.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Refusing all press access while a conspiracy narrative builds is a strategic error the industry appears unwilling to correct.
insights.locator: I reach out to a few operators

insights.claim: The physical footprint is a grievance in itself: in Data Center Alley a Vantage facility produces a constant low hum audible from the cul-de-sac across the street, and buildings loom over manicured suburban lawns.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Noise and visual scale are legally actionable nuisance grounds — concrete, provable harms that survive fact-checking in a way water-usage claims did not.
insights.locator: I end up driving around Data Center Alley

insights.claim: Utilities are becoming the flashpoint alongside operators, with a Coweta County, Georgia woman going viral on right-wing media alleging that the unpopular utility Georgia Power was using tactics to destroy her home to run transmission lines for a data center.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Transmission buildout, not just the data hall, is where eminent domain and viral grievance intersect — a distinct and underpriced risk for regulated utilities.
insights.locator: Shortly after I have coffee with Bailey

themes.theme: The intellectual lineage: Kaczynski to Humans First

insights.claim: Joe Allen's ideological formation traces directly to encountering Ted Kaczynski's 'Industrial Society and Its Future' at a community college writing lab in the late 1990s, and he writes that 'Uncle Ted made more sense than any peacenik or techie cares to admit.'
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: The movement's intellectual core is anti-industrial rather than pro-regulation, which limits how far accommodation or compliance can defuse it.
insights.quote: Uncle Ted made more sense than any peacenik or techie cares to admit
insights.locator: In his book, Allen vividly recalls

insights.claim: Kaczynski's critique has drifted into the mainstream from multiple directions: Luigi Mangione left a positive GoodReads review of the manifesto, PCMag published an essay titled 'The Unabomber Was Right,' and Ray Kurzweil wrote in 2000 that Kaczynski was 'correct on the deeply entangled nature of the benefits and risks' of technology.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Anti-technology sentiment has crossed from fringe to respectable across the political and industry spectrum — a durable shift in the operating environment for tech capital.
insights.locator: Twenty years later, Luigi Mangione

insights.claim: Anti-technology resistance is not confined to AI: a 2025 study found more than 450 counties and municipalities across nearly all states had solar or wind restrictions in place, a 16 percent year-over-year increase, and this resistance is baked into the anti-data-center movement's DNA.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Local-veto infrastructure opposition is generalizing across the energy transition, meaning both AI and clean energy buildouts face the same siting constraint.
insights.quote: A 2025 study found that more than 450 counties and municipalities across nearly all states had some sort of solar or wind restrictions in place, a 16 percent increase from the year before.
insights.locator: There are echoes of Kaczynski

insights.claim: The Make America Healthy Again movement is analytically the same phenomenon — a Kaczynski-flavored environmentalism holding that modern society poisons land, air, and water and that modern inventions like vaccines or antidepressants are harmful.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Treating MAHA, renewables opposition, and anti-data-center activism as one anti-modernity current gives a much better forecast of which technologies face political resistance next.
insights.locator: The Make America Healthy Again movement, too

insights.claim: Allen's core original concept is the 'inverse singularity' — that human intellect and creativity will collapse as people rely increasingly on AI for information, inverting the accelerationist promise.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A memorable counter-frame to the singularity narrative gives the movement its own vocabulary, which is what lets a critique spread beyond its originating subculture.
insights.locator: changing the topic to more interesting things

insights.claim: Allen's rhetorical method fuses metaphysical body horror with populist appeal, describing data centers as 'neurons of the Antichrist' and framing AI leaders' beliefs through a Heaven's Gate analogy in which humanity must shed physical bodies to ascend.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Religious framing gives the opposition emotional durability that cost-benefit arguments cannot dislodge, and it travels through church networks Bannon deliberately targeted.
insights.quote: Data centers, if you think about them as neurons of the Antichrist, that’s what we’re witnessing. The false messiah.
insights.locator: I ask him why he thinks people hate data centers

insights.claim: The reporter concedes the seemingly insane claims land because industry conduct corroborates them — Elon Musk owns a brain-chip implantation company and Sam Altman has blogged that humans will 'be the biological bootloader for digital intelligence and then fade into an evolutionary tree branch.'
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Executives' own published transhumanist statements are the movement's most effective recruiting material — reputational risk generated internally, not by opponents.
insights.quote: A lot of it can sound completely insane, until you remember: Oh, right. Elon Musk does own a brain-chip implantation company.
insights.locator: Allen’s lectures follow a familiar pattern

insights.claim: The Center for AI Safety recruited Joe Allen in late 2025 to advise a bipartisan group called Humans First, an explicit attempt by the technical AI safety establishment to acquire mass-movement reach it lacked.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: AI safety funding is now flowing into populist political organizing rather than research alone, which changes the constituency behind AI legislation.
insights.locator: In late 2025, the Center for AI Safety recruited Allen

insights.claim: The AI safety and ethics world is described as incestuous and inaccessible to non-specialists, with many high-profile researchers headquartered in a single Berkeley office block, split between annihilation-risk decelerationists and superintelligence-Nirvana accelerationists.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Extreme geographic and social concentration explains why the field completely missed the mass-public dimension of AI backlash — an information blind spot for anyone relying on it.
insights.quote: The world of AI safety and ethics is incestuous, almost completely inaccessible to normies, and full of people who live mostly in London or the Bay Area.
insights.locator: The world of AI safety and ethics

insights.claim: Allen has been rapidly legitimized inside the AI safety establishment — interviewing Gary Marcus, debating Max More and Nell Watson, and appearing on War Room with Max Tegmark on the same day Tegmark did an event with Bernie Sanders.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A single figure bridging Bannon's audience and Tegmark's shows the left-right AI-restriction coalition is real at the elite level too, not just among protesters.
insights.locator: Allen arrived in this world as an outsider

insights.claim: There is a competing left-wing anti-AI framework from scholars Timnit Gebru and Émile Torres, who argue AI development is largely an excuse for the wealthy to exploit existing inequalities and advance a eugenic agenda — and who have criticized the Center for AI Safety that funds Humans First.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: The left flank distrusts the safety establishment as much as the industry, which is the fault line most likely to prevent a unified national policy demand.
insights.locator: Right-wing anti-globalism isn’t the only way

insights.claim: Institutional religion has entered the field: Pope Leo XIV released an encyclical on AI, Magnifica Humanitas, in May, advising responsible development and the primacy of humanity.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Papal engagement gives AI restriction a global moral vocabulary and reach into constituencies far larger than any political movement.
insights.locator: There’s also the religious way

insights.claim: The movement now has a personal-harm narrative attached to AI products themselves, with Alicia Shamblin speaking at a Humans First event about her 23-year-old son Zane, who killed himself after hours of talking to ChatGPT, and whose parents are suing OpenAI.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Product liability litigation plus a sympathetic victim narrative is historically what converts diffuse opposition into binding regulation — the vector to watch for AI.
insights.locator: I park my car in the cul-de-sac

insights.claim: The movement's stated goal is a middle ground between total technological rejection and total capitulation to Big Tech, which the reporting suggests the American political system may not be equipped to deliver.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: If the moderate settlement is institutionally unreachable, outcomes polarize toward either blanket local bans or unmitigated buildout — both worse for planning than a negotiated regime.
insights.quote: The movement seems to envision a middle ground between rejecting technology wholesale—of truly Unabombering out—and rolling over and giving Big Tech everything it wants.
insights.locator: There’s a dream here
